claims.text: The initial materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles with a nominally single-phase, compositionally homogeneous solid-solution structure.
High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by the persistence of local short-range atomic order.
Short-range order can persist at elevated temperature in multi-principal-element alloys.
Persistent short-range order limits elemental diffusion at elevated temperature.
Persistent short-range order reduces the thermodynamic driving force for elemental segregation.
Persistent short-range order blocks kinetic pathways for elemental segregation.
Reduced diffusion and segregation preserve a single-phase, near-equiatomic nanoparticle state.
Nanoparticles lacking short-range order exhibit enhanced diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion in weakly ordered nanoparticles causes phase separation and morphological instability.
Strongly ordered nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional segregation than weakly ordered baseline nanoparticles during heating in reactive atmospheres.
Strongly ordered nanoparticles will retain their morphology better than weakly ordered baseline nanoparticles under the same conditions.
Less-controlled fabrication processes produce more random atomic distributions and lower initial short-range order.
The proposed ordering mechanism applies across catalytic temperatures of approximately 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures up to approximately 1923 K.
Substantially different nanoparticle size distributions or impurities can override the effect of short-range order on stability.
Reactive environmental chemistry can influence high-temperature chemical stability through diffusion-barrier formation or selective dissolution.
